title: Will the iPad Ever Be a Worthy Mac Replacement?
body:
iOS 9 brought us multitasking on iPad. Here's how far we've come since.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 10, 2026
            
            
                        Credit: David MAREUIL/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images/Lifehacker
                            
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET and Popular Science.For the first five years of its life, the iPad could only run one app at a time. Then, iOS 9 changed everything. That update, released 10 years ago this month, introduced multitasking to the Apple tablet for the first time. "Split View" let you run two apps side-by-side at once; "Slide Over" gave you quick access to a third app in an iPhone-style window; and Picture in Picture made it possible to watch a video while working on something else. In an article published at the time, these changes prompted Lifehacker to proclaim that "iOS 9 actually makes the iPad usable for work."In total, you could have up to four different windows on screen through this concoction of features, a huge improvement over the previous limit of "one." Coupled with the new keyboard shortcuts, iOS 9 transformed the iPad, and brought it closer to the laptop replacement so many users wanted it to be. "Closer" being the key word there. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Multitasking on iPad is still a work in progressWhile iOS 9 made it possible to focus on more than one app at a time, it didn't address other iPad limitations that made it difficult for computer users to fully make the switch. In the 11 years since that update, Apple has chipped away at those issues slowly but surely, while upgrading the iPad's hardware exponentially. In iOS 11, Apple made it easier to launch an app into Split View from the Dock, and introduced cross-app drag and drop. With iPadOS 13, Apple introduced a desktop-class version of Safari, and rolled out the Files app, which even supported hard drives and SD cards. iPadOS 15 improved Split View and Slide Over accessibility, and made it possible to multitask with multiple windows from one app. By iPadOS 16, it seemed like Apple had had enough of people complaining that the iPad wasn't enough like a Mac. This update introduced Stage Manager, which let users display and resize multiple floating app windows on screen. You could even connect your compatible iPad to an external monitor to run Stage Manager on both displays, just as you might connect a MacBook to a monitor. iPadOS 17 improved the experience again, adding support for FaceTime calls from external webcams, while last year's iPadOS 26 provided another overhaul, introducing the closest thing to a macOS-like window system yet, right down to the traffic-light window buttons. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We're at the point where, on the surface, the iPad can be considered Apple's answer to the touchscreen computer, especially when paired with a keyboard and trackpad. But in practical use, it's evident the iPad still isn't a Mac, even in cases where the iPad supports the apps and utilities you use on Mac. iPadOS doesn't feel designed for computer tasks; it feels like computer tasks were retrofitted to iPadOS. That doesn't mean things like multitasking and file support aren't welcome features, but the experience isn't as refined as it is on macOS. What's more, there is evidence Apple agrees the two devices are just too different, as rumors suggest the company might release a touchscreen MacBook as soon as next year. For me, iPadOS still feels at its best when I use one app at a time. All the above efforts to change its nature aside, that's probably because the iPad was originally designed that way. 
            
                        
                
            
                    
                                            
                
            
                Jake Peterson
                                    Senior Technology Editor

title: How to Get the Most Cloud Storage Possible for Free
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 15, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Cloud storage is likely an essential part of your data management strategy, whether you're just using Google Drive for documents or you back up everything to a remote service. You can get a significant amount of space for a reasonable monthly fee, but if you prefer not to pay, it's possible to combine free options and cobble together quite a bit of free storage—around 80GB (or more)—at no cost. A reminder: You shouldn't rely solely on cloud storage for your backups. Follow the 3-2-1 rule, which protects against a single point of failure, such as getting locked out of your account or issues with the service itself. Google: 15GB of free cloud storageThe most obvious option for free storage is Google Drive. Google offers up to 15GB of storage per account, though this is split across all Google apps, including Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos as well as Android backups. You could create multiple Google accounts, which would allow you to stack 15GB allotments. Note that Google recently introduced a 5GB free storage cap on some new accounts, though you can get around this by linking a phone number. 
Apple iCloud: 5GB of free cloud storageiCloud users automatically get 5GB of free storage, split across backups, photos, and files, as well as data from Messages, Mail, Contacts, FaceTime, voice memos, and Apple Invites. You can delete content to reduce the size of your iCloud backup to manage available storage space. The cheapest paid iCloud+ tier comes with 50GB storage for around $1 per month. Microsoft OneDrive: 5GB of free cloud storageSimilar to iCloud, OneDrive comes with 5GB of free cloud storage, and all you need is a Microsoft 365 account. This limit is shared across documents, files, and photos—Outlook gets a separate 15GB allotment. Box: 10GB of free cloud storageBox offers 10GB of secure storage on its free plan. There's a 250GB file upload limit, so this isn't the best option for media or larger files, plus you only get access to one file version. Free users do get 5 e-signature requests per month, so Box is a good choice for documents. Dropbox: 2GB of free cloud storageDropbox's free plan is limited to just 2GB of storage, which can be filled with photos, documents, and files from up to three devices. You can also use Dropbox to share files and collaborate with other users, and the service integrates with many third-party apps. Proton Drive: 5GB of free cloud storageProton is known for its privacy-focused products, so Proton Drive is a good choice for storing sensitive records like tax returns and legal documents. The free plan comes with 5GB of space, and your vault is end-to-end encrypted. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
MEGA: 20GB of free cloud storageMEGA allows a whopping 20GB of storage to free users with automatic backups and 100 file versions, making it a solid option for large archives and media. Other cloud storage services: Free storage amounts varyThere are a handful of other cloud storage providers that offer free plans without aggressive ads, major file size limitations, or serious privacy compromises. Other options include Sync.com (5GB), Icedrive (10GB), and pCloud (up to 10GB), though some users on Reddit have noted reliability and customer support concerns with these services. Password managers often include free storageYour password manager subscription may not technically be free, but if you're already paying for it, you may have some small amount of secure file storage at no additional cost. Bitwarden's Premium plan comes with 5 GB of encrypted storage, while many others (1Password, Proton Pass, and Dashlane, to name a few) include 1 GB. How to organize and maximize your free storage spaceIf you are using multiple cloud storage services, you can distribute different content types across each to maximize features and ease of access. Proton Drive and Sync.com are good choices for sensitive files you want to be sure are secure, though you can use a tool like Cryptomator (which is free and open source) to encrypt your vault before syncing to a service like Google Drive or Box. Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud are best for files and documents you need regularly, including items that require collaboration and sharing, as well as device backups. MEGA could be a solid option for cold storage—media that doesn't change or need to be accessed often. And Box is useful for smaller documents, like PDF records and receipts, given its individual file size limit.

                                            Senior Technology Editor

    Table of Contents
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET, and Popular Science.By 2017, some of us had been using iPhones for 10 years—a whole decade building muscle memory, all of it based around the Home button. Press once to go home; press twice to open the app switcher; long-press to call up Siri; press in tandem with the power button to take a screenshot: These actions became so innate, you didn't think twice about using them—at least, not until the Home button disappeared. 
That was the year Apple released the iPhone X, introducing the device's most radical change since its first iteration. (Perhaps only to be surpassed this year by the iPhone Duo.) It's funny to think about it today, but back in 2017, the iPhone X's single pane of glass was disruptive, to say the least. Where was the Home button? Without it, how could you do anything? That confusion inspired Lifehacker to publish "The iPhone X Gestures You Should Master," a guide to navigating your newly designed iPhone. 
We had to learn to swipe up from the bottom of the display to go home; to swipe along the bottom to switch from app to app; to swipe down from the top right to access Control Center; to swipe down from the top left to access Notification Center. We even had to relearn reachability: Instead of lightly double-tapping the Home button to bring the screen down, you had to swipe down on the bottom of the display. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Reviewing these things now, it all seems so obvious, even second nature. Nearly another decade has passed since we published that story, and by now, most iOS users are accostumed to a Home button-free life. But looking through the comments on this nearly decade-old piece, it's clear the transition was anything but smooth. One user complained about how smartphone gestures were making everything more confusing. Another bemoaned how switching between their iPhone and iPad meant jumping between two different gesture systems. Fast forward to 2026, and it's near impossible to imagine going back. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple didn't immediately stop making iPhones with Home buttons—it also released the iPhone 8 and 8 Plus the same year as the iPhone X—but the writing was on the wall. Soon after, only the SE line shipped with the old design, and even iPads adopted an edge-to-edge display. With the launch of the iPhone 16e in 2025, Apple officially retired the once-essential Home button. Though you can still buy and use second-hand devices that have one (the 2022 iPhone SE can even run iOS 27), it's clear the company has moved on, and the gestures once so foreign they once prompted us to publish a guide to their use are now as innate as doing things the old way. Perhaps in another 10 years, wearables and hand gestures will have changed everything again, and we'll look back with nostalgia on an era when we had to touch our devices at all.

title: I Tried 'Tailscale,' the Self-Hosted VPN Service That Makes It Look Like You're Always Home
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 15, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Tailscale has apps for all the major device platforms.
                                                    Credit: Tailscale
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Tailscale wasn't on my radar until a friend recently raved about its capabilities to me. Looking around the web, it seems the software has attracted a loyal following; perhaps part of the reason I hadn't come across it before is that it's not all that easy to understand what it does. Tailscale is technically a VPN (Virtual Private Network), but not in the way the term is typically used. Whereas something like NordVPN or ExpressVPN connects you to someone else's network to access the wider web, Tailscale does the opposite, and connects you to your own network from outside.
    
            
            Start your tailnet with one of the apps.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
"Remote access technology" has been around for years, of course, but it often involves a lot of detailed and technical setup steps—you want to be able to access your home network remotely without letting anyone else in, and that usually means some complicated configuration involving router settings and several third-party apps.There's none of that with Tailscale, and when you actually install the software, you quickly start to see what all the fuss is about. You can be sitting in a coffee shop or hotel room and have virtually the same access to your home network as you would if you were actually in your living room, which has all kinds of benefits, from file sharing to managing your smart home devices.
The obvious use case is remote access to a computer you have at home, without the layers of complexity or using another company's servers. Tailscale also makes it easier to access media servers you've set up with apps like Plex or Jellyfin, and smart home setups running through Home Assistant or another dashboard.
    
            
            You can be set up in minutes.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Everything is built on the open-source WireGuard VPN protocol, which creates private and encrypted links to all of the devices you want to connect to your network—your "tailnet." To add a new device, just install Tailscale on it, whether it's your phone on a 5G connection or a desktop computer set up at the office. Tailscale is free for personal use, which covers up to six individual users and an unlimited number of personal devices, though there are some limits: 50 tagged resources (always-on devices that need multi-user access, like a NAS box), and three Access Control List or ACL groups (for setting access permissions per user). Paid plans start at $8 per month.Putting Tailscale to the testThe ease of setup is one of the main appeals of Tailscale, and it couldn't be much more straightforward. Download the relevant app on whatever device you want to start with, create an account (you can sign in using a Google, Microsoft, GitHub, or Apple account), and you're up and running. I had a Windows PC, a MacBook, an Android phone, and an iPhone connected to my tailnet in a matter of minutes, with just a few taps and clicks required. There's also a web portal you can access to see all of the devices you've connected and what they're up to.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        

    
            
            The macOS app offers easy drag-and-drop file sharing.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
One improvement I noticed right away was the addition of Tailscale to the share sheet on Android and iOS, which meant I could quickly share photos and other files between all my devices in seconds (no AirDrop or Android Quick Share required). I could also instantly access the shared folders on my desktop and laptop computers from my phone.Something else you can do very easily is set up a remote access app on a phone and use it to connect directly to one of your computers in a different physical location, with no exposure to the wider internet and no advanced configuration required—Tailscale provides you with an IP address that looks like a local network. Any of your home computers can be configured as an exit node as well, which means internet traffic can be rerouted through it. If you're in a hotel, for example, you can use Tailscale as a secure tunnel back home, which means websites see you as visiting from home rather than an unrecognized hotel IP address.
    
            
            Taildrop lets you quickly share files between connected devices.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
There are some areas where Tailscale can improve (the Windows client isn't quite as straightforward to use as the macOS one), and it's fair to say at least some basic networking knowledge is required to get to grips with Tailscale, but in terms of software that's free and useful, it's hard to beat. I didn't dive into more advanced use cases involving NAS drives or home servers, as they're not something that I'm working with at the moment, but that's the next level of Tailscale capability

        The Linksys RE7000 Range Booster is designed to fill weak-signal gaps without changing your existing router, and it's currently on sale for just $27.99 as an open-box unit on StackSocial. Open box usually means the packaging has been handled or returned, but the unit itself has been checked and works like new. This model plugs straight into a wall outlet and keeps the top socket usable, so it doesn’t block access in tight spaces. In a typical home, Linksys claims coverage up to 2,500 square feet, though real-world results depend on walls and layout.Setup is simple: You press the WPS button to sync it with your router and use a phone or laptop to finish the process in a few minutes. It works with most routers, including those provided by internet service providers. Once it's in place, the extender works by pulling in your existing Wi-Fi signal and pushing it further into areas that struggle to stay connected. It supports AC1900 speeds across dual bands, which is enough for everyday use like streaming, browsing, or video calls, assuming your base connection is strong enough. MU-MIMO support helps when several people are connected at once, so one person streaming a show does not slow down someone else on a video call.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
There is also seamless roaming, which keeps your phone connected to the strongest signal automatically as you move around the house. The included Gigabit Ethernet port is also useful if you want a more stable wired connection for a console or desktop in a weak-signal area. That said, there are limits to what an extender like this can do—this is a Wi-Fi 5 extender, so it will not match the speeds or efficiency of newer Wi-Fi 6 or 7 hardware.
